2020 · IJCV · Benchmarks & Evals

The Open Images Dataset V4: Unified image classification, object detection, and visual relationship detection at scale

9,178,275 Creative-Commons Flickr images carrying three annotation types on the same pictures — 30.1M image-level labels across 19,794 classes, 15.4M bounding boxes across 600 classes, and 374,768 human-verified visual-relationship triplets — plus a custom detection metric built around the dataset's own non-exhaustive labeling.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

By 2018 the field had three separate, task-specific benchmarks it kept stacking together by hand: ImageNet for image classification, COCO for detection and segmentation, and PASCAL VOC or ILSVRC-Detection as the older detection standard. Each was built by a different pipeline, on a different image pool, with a different notion of what counts as "annotated." None of them let a researcher train or evaluate classification, detection, and a third task — visual relationship detection, i.e. recognizing that a box labeled man is holding a box labeled guitar — on the identical set of images. Cross-task transfer, joint training, or studying how one annotation type could bootstrap another was structurally awkward: the datasets simply didn't overlap enough to try.

The paper also targets a subtler gap: image sourcing bias. Prior datasets were frequently built by querying search engines or curated photo pools for a predefined list of class names — a design choice that, the authors argue, bakes in whatever assumptions went into the query list and skews toward images search engines already rank highly (which tend to be simple, single-subject shots). Open Images instead pulls from all Creative-Commons-Attribution-licensed Flickr uploads with no predefined class list, then explicitly discards images that also appear elsewhere on the web, on the theory that this favors complex, multi-object scenes over simple, single-subject stock-search imagery.

Finally, existing detection metrics assumed something Open Images' own annotation process couldn't guarantee: that every instance of every class in an image is labeled. Standard PASCAL VOC/COCO mAP treats an undetected-but-unlabeled object as ambiguous at best; a dataset with 19,794 image-level classes and incomplete-by-necessity coverage needed an evaluation protocol that didn't quietly penalize models for being right about things nobody verified.

// how it works

The method

Image acquisition. Starting in November 2015, the authors identified all CC-BY-licensed Flickr images, downloaded originals at two resolutions (a 1,600px-longest-side "1600HQ" and a ~300,000-pixel "300K"), captured attribution metadata, ran safety filters (Flickr's own plus Google SafeSearch), removed near-duplicates by low-level visual similarity, and — the deliberate bias-reduction step — removed any image that also appears elsewhere on the web. The result: 9,178,275 images split into train (9,011,219), validation (41,620), and test (125,436).

Classes. The label vocabulary — 19,794 image-level classes — was drawn from JFT, Google's internal ~300M-image dataset, spanning coarse object classes, fine-grained breeds/models, scenes, events, and materials/attributes. Of those, 600 classes with a clear spatial extent were designated "boxable" and organized into a class hierarchy (e.g. Football Helmet and Bicycle Helmet are both subclasses of Helmet) — a structure the detection metric later depends on.

Image-level labels. Manually checking 19,794 classes per image at human scale is infeasible, so the pipeline is computer-assisted: an Inception-V2-based classifier trained on JFT proposes candidate labels (confidence > 0.5 for validation/test; a stratified, logit-binned sampling scheme across dozens of classifier variants for train, to get a spread of easy/hard positives and negatives), and humans then verify each candidate as positive or negative. Verification used two annotator pools — a majority-of-7 crowdsource pool and an internal pool (1-3 annotators depending on class difficulty) — with crowd-sourced labels making up about 20% of train verifications but under 1% of validation/test verifications.

Bounding boxes. Annotators worked one class at a time, shown a manually-curated "perfect box" example plus common-mistake examples before each session, in part to control for effects the authors explicitly call out — e.g., what counts as a human hand's extent differs by region. 90% of boxes came from extreme clicking (Papadopoulos et al. 2017): annotators click the top/bottom/left/right-most physical points of an object rather than imaginary tight-box corners, cutting average draw time from 25.5s to 7.4s per box. The remaining 10% came from box verification series: a Faster-RCNN/Inception-ResNet detector (bootstrapped via weakly-supervised knowledge transfer, then periodically retrained on accepted boxes) proposes a box, a human accepts or rejects it against a 0.7 IoU threshold, up to four attempts; acceptance rose from 48% (initial detector) to 70% (final, retrained detector) over the course of annotation. Hierarchical de-duplication removes a redundant parent-class box (e.g. don't box both animal and zebra for the same instance). Boxes also carry five attributes — GroupOf (5+ occluding instances in one box), Occluded, Truncated, Depiction, and Inside.

Visual relationships. Rather than free-form region descriptions (the approach Visual Genome and the VRD dataset took), Open Images leverages its own bounding boxes: for a candidate triplet ⟨class1, relationship, class2⟩, any pair of boxes whose classes match class1 and class2 (generally two different classes, not the same one) and that still overlap once each box is enlarged by 20% is shown to a human annotator, who verifies whether the relationship actually holds. 326 candidate triplets were selected (co-occurring frequently enough, not trivially inferable from co-occurrence alone, and not "part-of" relations); 287 of them had at least one verified train-split instance. Acceptance rates were deliberately low across the board — 58.9% for the easiest relation ("at"), 27.9% for the median ("holds"), 2.3% for the hardest ("under"), 28.2% overall — which the paper reads as evidence the selected relationships aren't trivially guessable from spatial co-occurrence.

The mAPOI metric. Standard PASCAL VOC 2012 mAP assumes exhaustive per-image annotation, a class-hierarchy-free label set, and no ambiguous group regions — none of which hold for Open Images. The paper's evaluation protocol (used for its own detection challenge) makes three changes: (1) non-exhaustive labeling — ignore any detection of a class that has neither a positive nor a negative image-level label on that image, so a correct-but-unverified prediction isn't scored as a false positive; a detection of a negatively-labeled class is still a false positive, and IoU > 0.5 against ground truth is still required for a true positive on a positively-labeled class; (2) class hierarchy — a non-leaf class's average precision is computed over the union of its own instances and all its subclasses' instances, so a model must output a detection for every ancestor class in the hierarchy to get full credit; (3) group-of boxes — a single box covering 5+ occluded instances is scored as one true positive if any detection lands inside it (weight w=1, the setting used in the final metric), rather than penalizing per hidden instance.

// what they found

The results

Scale, by annotation type and split. Image-level labels: 5,655,108 train images carry human-verified labels (13,444,569 positive + 14,449,720 negative, averaging 2.4 positive / 2.6 negative per image), versus 41,620 validation and 125,436 test images (365,772 / 185,618 and 1,105,052 / 562,347 positive/negative respectively, averaging 8.8 positive labels per image in both — denser because validation/test candidates were generated exhaustively per-class rather than via train's stratified sampling). Bounding boxes: 1,743,042 train images carry boxes (14,610,229 boxes, 8.4/image) plus the full validation (204,621 boxes, 4.9/image) and test (625,282 boxes, 5.0/image) splits, all restricted to the 600 boxable classes. Visual relationships: 374,768 train-split triplet instances, 3,991 validation, 12,314 test — 329 distinct triplet types (287 two-object relations + 42 attribute triplets like ⟨chair, is, wooden⟩) spanning 57 object classes and 5 attribute types.

Against prior detection datasets. Restricting to the 1,910,098 images that carry boxes, Open Images offers 15,440,132 boxes across 600 classes (8.1/image) versus COCO 2017's 886,284 boxes across 80 classes on 123,287 images (7.2/image), PASCAL 2012's 27,450 boxes on 11,540 images (2.4/image), and ILSVRC-2014-Detection's 534,309 boxes on 476,688 images (1.1/image) — 17.4× more boxes than COCO specifically, and roughly the same box-density-per-image as COCO. 11 Open Images classes individually have more instances than COCO's single largest class (person, at 257,253); the aggregated "person"-family classes (person, woman, man, girl, boy — each object gets only its single leafmost label) total 3,505,362 instances. At the long-tail end, 517 Open Images classes still out-number COCO's rarest class (198 instances) and 417 out-number ILSVRC's rarest (502 instances).

Box and label quality. A human expert checked 100 images each for the first 150 boxable classes in alphabetical order (>26,000 boxes): box precision 97.7%, recall 98.2%, with the remaining precision error split between geometrically imprecise boxes (1.1%) and wrong-class-label boxes (1.1%). Semantic-class confusion concentrated in a few classes — bidet (86% error, confused with toilets), cello (55%, confused with violins), and coffee table (35%, an inherently ambiguous category) were the worst three of the 150 examined. Box attribute precision/recall was high for GroupOf (94.2%/95.3%), Occluded (98.6%/98.4%), Truncated (99.7%/97.0%), and Depiction (96.7%/92.2%); Inside was noisier (66.7% precision, 90.3% recall) but also rare. Independently, re-drawing 50,000 extreme-clicking boxes gave 0.87 average IoU agreement with the originals (versus 0.88 reported for PASCAL); re-drawing a 1% sample of box-verification-series boxes gave 0.77 IoU — and training identical Faster-RCNN detectors on verified-vs-manually-drawn boxes for the same object instances produced detection performance within 0.001 mAPOI of each other. Image-level label recall — how many true boxable-class instances actually got any label at all — was measured at 43% overall, 59% excluding PASCAL-style "difficult" (very small/occluded/truncated) objects, versus an 83% recall the paper quotes for COCO; the paper attributes the gap to Open Images covering 7.5× more classes.

Baseline models. For image classification (Inception-ResNet-V2, trained on classes with ≥100 positive train examples — 7,186 classes — evaluated with per-class AP on the 4,728 classes with >0 test examples), classifier mAP rose monotonically as more human-verified labels were used for fine-tuning (1% through 100% of train), and rose further once explicit human-verified negative labels were added on top of positives — the paper's evidence that its negative-label annotations do real work, not just its positives. For detection, a Faster-RCNN/Inception-ResNetV2 model (63,947,366 parameters, 0.455s/image on a Titan X Pascal) and an SSD/MobileNetV2 model (14,439,167 parameters, 0.024s/image) were trained on four increasing training subsets — 10k, 100k, 1M, and all 14.6M boxes. Faster-RCNN kept improving through the full 14.6M-box subset; the smaller SSD saturated around 1M boxes, which the paper reads as evidence that Open Images' scale mainly benefits higher-capacity models.

Visual relationship detection baselines (Table 15, on the OI test set) combined two frequency-prior baselines — FREQ and FREQ-OVERLAP, both variants of p(S,P,O|I) = p(S|I)·p(P|O,S)·p(O|S,I) computed from train-set co-occurrence statistics — against BAR-CNN, a model that predicts subjects then attends to each to predict connected objects:

BaselinemAPOI Challenge score
FREQ5.3618.93
FREQ-OVERLAP8.1921.47
FREQ (RetinaNet+ResNet50 detections)5.6819.01
FREQ-OVERLAP (RetinaNet+ResNet50)8.1221.02
BAR-CNN (RetinaNet+ResNet50)14.6327.60

The "OI Challenge score" column is a weighted average of relationship-detection mAP, phrase-detection mAP, and Recall@50 — not the same metric as the "mAP" column. BAR-CNN roughly doubles the frequency baselines' mAP, which the paper takes as evidence that visual relationships need more than object-detection-plus-co-occurrence-priors to predict well.

What the unified annotations enable. Two demonstration experiments exploit having all three annotation types on the same images. First, fine-grained detection: image-level labels that are semantically more specific than a boxable parent class (e.g. Labrador under Dog) get transferred onto that parent's box when only one instance of the parent class appears in the image. Trained this way, a single Faster-RCNN detector reached 0.287 mAP over 57 Car subclasses, 0.231 over 61 Cat subclasses, 0.272 over 33 Dog subclasses, and 0.594 over 102 Flower subclasses — versus <0.05 mAP for every uniform-random, most-common-subclass, or prior-based-random baseline in every one of those four rows. Some individual subclasses did far better still — Ferrari (0.638 mAP), Land Rover (0.620), Schnauzer (0.542). Second, zero-shot visual relationship detection: bounding-box classes with no relationship annotations of their own (48 such classes, filtered to those with ≥10 test-split relationship instances) were paired with existing relationship types via their box co-occurrence, yielding 194 new triplet types and 5,983 zero-shot test annotations. A single BAR-CNN model reached 40.61/40.93 R@50/R@100 on the full (supervised+zero-shot) relationship-detection test set but only 7.68/7.70 R@50/R@100 restricted to zero-shot-only triplets — for phrase detection, 43.65/43.86 versus 10.98/11.08. The paper's own reading: zero-shot VRD "can be tackled to a reasonable degree but the gap to the supervised results is still very large."

// does it hold up?

The eval read

Open Images V4 is unusually candid about its own limitations by dataset-paper standards — it reports a 43-59% label-recall figure against its own held-out expert audit, states plainly that 90% of boxes came from a technique it "co-invented" partway through annotation (extreme clicking) after starting with a different technique (box verification series) for the first 1.5M boxes, and explicitly benchmarks its own custom mAPOI metric against vanilla PASCAL-style mAP rather than quietly swapping one in for the other. That candor is real, but it also surfaces places the paper's own numbers raise questions it doesn't answer.

Start with the candidate-label pipeline itself: every image-level label the dataset ships began life as a machine prediction from an Inception-V2 classifier (or, for train, "dozens of" Inception/ResNet-family classifiers) trained on JFT, filtered to a confidence threshold before any human ever saw it. A verification-only pipeline can correct a machine's false positives, but it structurally cannot surface a true positive the underlying classifier never proposed — a form of coverage bias baked in before annotation begins. The paper documents that its class frequencies are heavily skewed (the Fig. 3 word cloud of infrequent image-level classes, the log-scale Fig. 17 per-class box-count curve) and separately reports that classification mAP on the 600 boxable classes runs higher than mAP on the full 19,794-class set — attributed to boxable classes being "basic-level categories" rather than the fine-grained breeds and abstract concepts the wider set includes — but at no point does the paper check whether the candidate-generation step itself under-proposes labels for classes the JFT classifier recognizes less well, as opposed to those classes genuinely appearing less often in the Flickr photo pool.

Second, the box-quality headline — 97.7% precision, 98.2% recall — comes from auditing "the first 150 boxable classes sorted by alphabetical order," not a random or frequency-weighted sample of the 600. Whether alphabetically-early class names (roughly the letters A through C-ish) are representative of quality across the full boxable vocabulary is untested; the paper doesn't flag the sampling scheme as a limitation anywhere in Section 4 or the conclusion.

Third, on distribution: the paper documents "cultural differences" in how annotators interpreted class boundaries — its own example is that a human hand's extent (does it include the whole arm?) varies by region — but never characterizes the geographic, linguistic, or demographic distribution of either the ~9M source photographers or the annotator pools resolving those differences. A dataset explicitly built by keeping only Flickr-hosted, CC-BY-licensed, non-search-engine-visible images is a specific and non-random slice of photography, and the paper doesn't quantify what that slice looks like.

baselines

Current-for-2018 and reasonably matched (Faster-RCNN/Inception-ResNetV2 vs SSD/MobileNetV2 for detection; FREQ/FREQ-OVERLAP vs BAR-CNN for relationships), but the two detection backbones differ by 4.4× in parameter count, so the comparison of which detector benefits more from scale across the 10k→14.6M-box sweep conflates data volume with model capacity rather than isolating either one.

contamination

Not train/test leakage in the LLM sense, but an analogous scoring quirk: since only 43-59% of true boxable-class instances carry any image-level label, and the mAPOI protocol explicitly ignores detections of unlabeled classes rather than scoring them as errors, a model is neither rewarded nor punished for the ~41-57% of cases nobody verified — a fundamentally different scoring regime from a benchmark like COCO that assumes near-exhaustive coverage (its own quoted 83% recall). The paper does offer a partial mitigation: it notes the incomplete recall is "partially compensated by having explicit negative image labels," which support proper discriminative training, and stresses that once an image carries a positive label for a class, every instance of that class in the image is then boxed — "fully annotated" along that dimension (98.2% recall, Table 12). Neither point closes the mAPOI gap this critique is about, though: negative labels help train a classifier, not a detector's scoring at eval time, and the 98.2%-recall boxing guarantee only applies to classes an image already has a positive label for — it says nothing about the 41-57% of instances that never got a label, positive or negative, in the first place, which is exactly the population mAPOI excludes from scoring by an explicitly stated ignore rule.

what's missed

Whether the JFT-classifier-driven candidate stage under-proposes classes it doesn't already recognize well; whether the alphabetically-sampled 150-class quality audit generalizes to the full 600; any accounting of the source-image or annotator population's geographic/demographic composition.

would raise confidence

A random (not alphabetical) resample for the box- and label-quality audits; an ablation isolating candidate-generator coverage from human-verification accuracy; and a shared-backbone re-run of the detector data-scaling experiment so architecture capacity isn't entangled with training-set size.

// bottom line

The scale claims hold up under their own accounting — 15.4M boxes across Open Images' full 600-class boxable set versus COCO's 886,284 boxes across its 80 classes (17.4× more), a genuinely unified triple-annotation scheme, and a metric that's transparent about departing from PASCAL-style mAP rather than hiding the departure. What the paper doesn't do is turn its own candor about label recall and cultural variance into an actual audit of where the dataset's coverage gaps come from, leaving whether a class is rare in the world or rare because the labeling pipeline under-proposed it, and who is and isn't represented in 9M Flickr photos, as open questions a reader has to bring their own priors to.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. Open Images V4 unifies three annotation types — 30.1M image-level labels (19,794 classes), 15.4M bounding boxes (600 classes, 17.4× COCO's total box count across COCO's 80 classes), and 374,768 train-split visual-relationship triplets (329 distinct types, 57 classes) — on the same 9.18M Creative-Commons Flickr images, letting cross-task and joint-annotation experiments run on a single image pool for the first time at this scale.
  2. Its evaluation protocol, mAPOI, deliberately departs from PASCAL/COCO mAP in three ways — ignoring detections of unannotated classes, crediting a class hierarchy, and scoring group-of boxes as a single true positive — a defensible fix for genuinely non-exhaustive labels, but one that makes raw mAP numbers non-comparable across benchmarks without re-deriving them under a shared protocol.
  3. Quality is measured and reported honestly (97.7%/98.2% box precision/recall; 43-59% label recall against COCO's quoted 83%) but the audit itself samples the boxable-class vocabulary alphabetically rather than randomly or by frequency, and the paper never investigates whether its machine-proposed-then-verified labeling pipeline systematically under-covers classes the underlying JFT classifier doesn't already recognize well.
